claims.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, passed through Cairo on pilgrimage to Mecca
claims.evidence: Headnote: 'the visit to Cairo in 1324 by the King of Mali, Mansa Musa'

claims.text: Al-Umari wrote that he gave away so much gold that its price in Egypt fell for years
claims.evidence: Final paragraphs: gold's price fell and stayed low 'for about twelve years'

claims.text: Timbuktu grew into a centre of Islamic learning
claims.evidence: Last paragraph: Timbuktu 'drew scholars from all over the Islamic world'

claims.text: Sijilmasa stood at the northern edge of the desert; Tadmekka and Timbuktu at the southern edge, linked to the Niger; the gold was prized for purity and minted into coins
claims.evidence: Second and third paragraphs give the three towns, the Niger link, purity and minting

claims.text: Mali spread over lands that today lie in Mauritania, Senegal, Mali, Niger and beyond

claims.text: He stayed in Cairo, where he met the sultan, al-Malik al-Nasir
claims.evidence: First paragraph of the account names the sultan and describes the audience. The draft said 'Mamluk sultans', which no listed source says; reworded.

claims.text: He had the Djinguereber mosque built with scholars and an architect from Andalusia who came back with him

claims.text: Al-Umari was a 14th-century Arab historian who wrote at least a decade after the visit
claims.evidence: Headnote says he came to Cairo years later; his text says prices had stayed low 'about twelve years until this day'

claims.text: Musa said he came for the pilgrimage and nothing else, sent unworked gold to the treasury, and gave gold to every emir and officeholder
claims.evidence: The emir's report in the first paragraph, and the 'flooded Cairo with his benefactions' paragraph

claims.text: The mithqal was worth at least 25 dirhams before the visit and no more than 22 for about twelve years after
claims.evidence: Last paragraph gives 25 dirhams, 22 dirhams and twelve years

claims.text: Excavations at Sijilmasa, Gao and Tadmekka found glazed pottery, glass, beads and silk
claims.evidence: Paragraph on archaeological discoveries, and the caption listing finds from Essouk-Tadmekka

claims.text: Finds in Mali suggest Arabic was spreading south of the Sahara by the 900s
claims.evidence: Section 'All that Glitters': Esmeralda Kale on Arabic 'making inroads' in the 10th century

claims.text: Modern accounts repeat 8,000 courtiers, 12,000 servants and a hundred camel loads of gold, and call him the richest person who ever lived
claims.evidence: Second and fourth paragraphs give all three numbers and the 'richest person in history' claim

claims.text: Numbers like these are hard to verify, and wealth across seven centuries cannot be compared in any exact way
claims.evidence: No listed source doubts the numbers; this one repeats them as fact. Needs a source that questions the entourage figures or the wealth comparison.
